P1.evidence: The best opening in the batch. Setter notes genuinely read back, twice - 'I already heard a few things from Derek' and then used specifically at 00:06:17: 'I heard something from Derek, I think, of your energy sort of not being as how you would want it to be. Is that true?' The frame ran to two of four parts - 'where you are, where you want to go. See if we can really help you out with that... If not, perfectly fine, and I'll still point you in the best possible direction' - with what's in the way and what you need both missing. Frame agreement and the open question both clean.

P2.evidence: Nutrition was outstanding - the diet was asked for directly and then the frequency was pinned down with 'is that like once a day, once a week, once a month?', producing the single most useful admission on the call ('I'm eating like that every day'). Energy was probed properly too. But height was never asked at all, age was asserted rather than asked, and the two structural misses are serious. Health conditions and hereditary risk were never raised despite the prospect volunteering that his father had a multi-year terminal illness that ended two years ago - nobody asked what it was. And no question was ever put about injuries, chronic pain, medications or supplements, on a call where the prospect was on day three of an extended fast and self-administering peptides and research compounds. Sleep came out in detail but entirely unprompted.

P3.evidence: The strongest Phase 3 in the batch. The bridge question landed properly - 'Why did you decide again to actually go back into it and dedicate yourself to it again? Like, what was that driver for you?' - and the five-years-out question got him to 47 and then to 'I would love to be an active 60-year-old.' The reflect-back was genuinely good work: the rep had ordered the goals as weight first, the prospect corrected him with 'I'd probably say energy would be above the weight loss', and the rep rebuilt the summary around energy with weight as the by-product. The kids-on-shoulders detail, which is the real why, was volunteered rather than asked for.

P4.evidence: The history was traced well - keto, intermittent fasting, the hypertrophy phases, 170 to 185 to 211 - but the root cause was left on the table. The prospect handed him the exact opening at 00:19:12: 'Took a year off, and then hit it again for a good nine months, year off, and then about six to eight months again, and then I have no idea why I stopped, but I really don't.' The rep's response was to turn away from it: 'Biggest question might be why you started again.' Nobody ever asked why it did not stick, or what is actually in the way. Worse for the outcome, the prospect framed his own gap as missing information - 'I would love to have a couple of science-backed tools' - and the rep agreed with that frame rather than running P4f, which is the one line written to break it: 'the information isn't the problem. Why can't you stick to it on your own?' Validating the tools frame is what made a $199 information product a credible substitute forty minutes later.

P5.evidence: Asked and then re-asked when the first version was misread: 'Would you be willing to have the same weight, stay in the same position for the next few years, or are you absolutely not willing to have that happen?' The answer was genuinely honest and genuinely negative - 'I am willing to be the same weight and have the energy. For one more year' - and the follow-up 'Why?' was put. But the rep then absorbed the one-year timeline as though it were urgency ('if you're like, I need to have a change in a year, then it sounds like it's an urgency for you') rather than working on it, and no line in the sand was ever asked for.

P6.evidence: The belief question ran - 'do you feel like that can actually get you to the point where you have that more energy?' - and came back qualified: 'Theoretically, yes, I have, I can't necessarily see it just yet until you guys show me the details on it.' The rep acknowledged the hesitation, softened the question to 'do you feel like just theoretically... this is something I see myself doing?', took the softer yes, and went to price. The script is explicit that hesitation sends you back to Phase 5, and there were two open hesitations here - the theoretical yes and the earlier willingness to settle for another year. Neither was worked. The go-all-in question was never asked in its scripted form.

P11.evidence: A close was attempted in that the offer and price were presented, but the prospect declined on price immediately and the call never reached agreement, so no payment or onboarding step was available to run.

objection_plays.detail: The isolate was done properly and is the best example of it in the batch: 'it sounds like it's a yes, I want to do it, money is just limiting it at the moment.' 'Yes.' After that the play stopped. There was no HOW-not-SHOULD-I reframe, no 'most clients pay upfront but for some we break it up', no permission question, and none of the six financial-picture questions beyond a single vague 'what do you have available'. Critically, no payment plan was offered at all - the rep cut the price instead, twice, disclosing a $3,000 version and then a $1,000 product within ninety seconds of the objection.

Known script gap two, and the cleanest instance of it in the corpus: 'One-on-one trainings, coaching programs are around $129 to $199 a month. So that's what I kind of thought you guys were at.' There is no scripted play. The rep improvised reasonably - authority positioning on Trevor, a market-rate reframe ('It's usually around $3,000 for six months, $3,000, $4,000'), and the travel-portability differentiator, which the prospect actually picked up and said was Primal's edge. He then gave it all back by offering to research the competitor and telling the prospect to buy them if the price was real.

No clinical screening step exists and none was improvised. The prospect was on day three of a multi-day fast with a stated intention of seven to ten days, self-administering peptides and research compounds, and about to be programmed three to four cardio-heavy kettlebell sessions a week. The rep's only response to the fasting was to endorse it: 'Trevor loves overall fasting as well, he does it every month, so that's definitely something that the two of you will bond over.'

notes: Technically the best-run call in the batch through Phase 3, and it lost anyway - which is the point. The two failures that decided it are both coachable: he turned away from 'I have no idea why I stopped' instead of opening it, and he accepted the prospect's own framing that what he needs is more tools, which is precisely the frame P4f exists to break and which made a $199 information product a rational substitute. Then at the objection he cut price rather than structuring payment, and disclosed two cheaper tiers to a prospect who had already told him money was the only blocker.
